_about: The questions the alert-triage receiver asks Jev about every alert. Edit the wording here to try your own; no code change is needed.
Point ALERT_TRIAGE_QUESTIONS at another file to keep several versions side by side, and restart the receiver after an edit.
Backticked names such as `alert` and `recent_alerts` refer to fields of the state Jev is sent; keep them.
Questions used only by the offline experiments are in experiments/experiment_questions.json.

urgency._used_by: every alert; urgency x user impact sets the page order
urgency.question: Does `alert` report a real production problem that an on-call engineer needs to act on now?

context_rules._about: Appended to the question, in this order, when that context is sent
context_rules.recent_alerts: Judge `alert` on its own evidence first. An alert in `recent_alerts` counts only if it is on the same service as `alert`, or on a service that `alert`'s service calls or is called by; ignore the rest, however many there are.
context_rules.recent_deploys: A rollout in `recent_deploys` counts only if it is of `alert`'s own service. A marginal crossing just after such a rollout is its normal warm-up; a severe one points to a bad rollout.
context_rules.alert_states: Each recent alert has a `state`. A resolved alert does not by itself show that a problem is still under way.

urgency.yes: A genuine fault in production, or a symptom of an incident that is under way: sustained errors, an outage, a crash loop, a resource about to run out
urgency.no: Noise: a marginal or brief threshold crossing, the expected effect of a healthy rollout or a scheduled batch job, a non-production environment, or nothing that needs doing now
urgency.no_when_recent_alerts_are_sent: even while unrelated alerts are firing on other services

user_impact._used_by: every alert, in the same request as urgency: shown beside it
user_impact.question: How much end-user traffic is affected right now by what `alert` describes? Judge `alert` itself; recent alerts and deploys are context for it.

levels.name: no user traffic
levels.description: No end-user traffic passes through what `alert` describes: a background or batch job, an internal tool, the monitoring itself, or a non-production environment such as staging

levels.name: users not affected yet
levels.description: A production component that user-facing services depend on is affected, but user requests are still answered normally for now: a degraded replica, a dependency with spare capacity, a resource trending towards its limit

levels.name: some users affected
levels.description: Some end-user requests are slower or failing: a user-facing service shows raised latency or a minority of its requests erroring

levels.name: users broadly affected
levels.description: End-user requests are failing broadly, or a user-facing service is down
